claims.text: Courthouse News reports the Supreme Court of Texas heard argument over whether a party should be allowed to submit a deposition transcript generated with AI as evidence.
claims.quote: The Texas Supreme Court heard arguments Tuesday over whether an individual should be allowed to submit an AI-generated transcript of a deposition as evidence.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Courthouse News reports the case began as a Montgomery County man's wrongful termination claim against his former employer.
claims.quote: The case concerns a Montgomery County man’s wrongful termination claim against his former employer.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Courthouse News reports the trial court in Montgomery County struck the transcript from the record in April 2025 because no certified shorthand reporter prepared it.
claims.quote: The trial court in Montgomery County struck the AI-generated transcript the employee submitted from the record back in April 2025 because the transcript was not prepared by a certified shorthand reporter.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Courthouse News reports the Texas Court of Appeals for the Ninth District denied the employee in an unsigned ruling. It says that court found the issue was the uncertified written transcript generated with AI, not the content of the deposition or its use as evidence.
claims.quote: In their unsigned denial of his appeal, the Texas Court of Appeals for the Ninth District reaffirmed that the issue was not with the content of the deposition or the use of the deposition as evidence, but merely with the use of an uncertified, AI-generated written transcript.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions
claims.note: Appeal is Courthouse News's word. The schedule lists a petition for writ of mandamus (c23).

claims.text: Courthouse News reports the company did not object to the transcription software at the deposition and asked the trial court to strike the transcript several weeks later.
claims.quote: However, the company did not object to the use of the transcription software at the time of the deposition, only asking the trial court to strike it several weeks later.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Courthouse News reports Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock observed at argument that paying a certified reporter, or letting the depositions go ahead this way, would have been cheaper. He then asked why the case was before the court at all, Courthouse News reports.
claims.quote: Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock noted it would have just been cheaper for the employee’s counsel to pay for the certified reporter, or it would have been cheaper for the company’s counsel to just let the depositions happen this way. “Why are we here?” he asked.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Justice Jane Bland asked at argument where the court would find the assurance of a human being standing behind the transcribed product, Courthouse News reports.
claims.quote: Where are we going to get that peace, of a human being standing behind the transcribed product?
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Bradley Snead argued for the employee that the deposition's video recording is certified and so the transcript does not have to be, Courthouse News reports.
claims.quote: Snead argued that because the deposition’s video recording is certified, the transcript does not have to be.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions
supporting_quotes: Justice Jane Bland pressed Bradley Snead, an attorney for the employee’s side from Houston-based Wright Close, on whether the AI-generated transcript was true and correct.

claims.text: Snead told the court it can create more rules if it wants. He said that under the current rules a party is allowed to do this, Courthouse News reports.
claims.quote: “If the court wants to create more rules, they can. But under the current rules, you are allowed to do this.”
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: The employer's lawyer Stephanie L. Bryant argued that using AI programs to produce written transcripts and take depositions this cheaply would exponentially increase discovery costs, Courthouse News reports.
claims.quote: the use of these AI programs to generate written transcripts and do these depositions this cheaply is going to affect litigation. It’s going to exponentially increase discovery costs.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Bryant said she had no issue with lawyers using their own in-house AI software. She argued that a third-party AI transcription platform like the one the employee used raises substantial security and confidentiality questions, Courthouse News reports. She said it would not be allowed under current Texas rules.
claims.quote: Bryant insisted she had no issue with litigants or attorneys using their own in-house AI software, but that using a third-party AI transcription platform like the employee did in this case raises substantial security and confidentiality questions, and that as such, it would not be allowed under current Texas rules of procedure.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Justice J. Brett Busby asked Bryant at argument whether the court's proportionality rules would take care of her concern about costs, Courthouse News reports.
claims.quote: Justice J. Brett Busby pressed Bryant on her assertion of increased costs for defendants and reduced costs for plaintiffs. “Wouldn’t our proportionality rules take care of that?”
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Justice Kyle Hawkins said at argument that the other side can point out an error and watch the video, Courthouse News reports. He said he didn't see what the issue is.
claims.quote: If they submit the AI transcript, you have the chance to say, ‘That’s wrong, there’s an error in the transcript, and we’ve got the video and we can just watch that.’ I don’t see what the issue is.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Hawkins asked at argument why the court should set aside what he called an efficient, cost-effective tool, Courthouse News reports.
claims.quote: He also questioned why they should set aside the use of “this efficient, cost-effective tool,” as he described the AI transcription platform.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Justice Evan Young said at argument that the court has escape hatches. He named the actual recording and a judge's power to order a certified shorthand reporter, Courthouse News reports.
claims.quote: “We have all of these escape hatches,” Young continued. “We have the actual recording. We have the ability of the judge to say ‘Okay, there’s just too much about this. I want a certified shorthand reporter to do this.’
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions

claims.text: Courthouse News read the argument as showing the justices seemed inclined to allow AI transcripts where verified video recordings act as escape hatches. That is the outlet's reading, not a ruling.
claims.quote: Texas Supreme Court justices seemed inclined to allow AI-generated transcripts for witness depositions where verified video recordings can act as "escape hatches" to ensure accuracy.
claims.document: Texas high court toys with AI transcripts for witness depositions
claims.note: The outlet's characterisation, never a ruling.
